clue.text: Like unpolluted water River Board wanted

parts.note: the Po is the great river of northern Italy
a table is a board, as in 'board and lodging' or a table laid for meals

explanation.surface: A water authority insists on clean rivers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'River Board' looks like an official body; split it into its two words. 'wanted' only joins the pieces to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Drinkable water is described as fit to drink, which is exactly what the word means.

clue.text: Old man's weapons demanded by sentries

parts.note: pa is an informal word for father, an old man
swords are weapons

explanation.surface: Dad's swords are requisitioned by guards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old man' is the familiar term for a father, PA.
explanation.definitionFit: Sentries challenge anyone approaching and require the secret words before letting them pass.

clue.text: Gradually decrease two types of spin

parts.note: a spun coin may come down tails
off spin is a type of bowling in cricket

explanation.surface: Advice to slow down by varying how you spin.
explanation.walkthrough: One spin is a tossed coin landing tails; the other is off spin, a cricket bowler's ball that turns into the batsman from the off side.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that tails off dwindles gradually until it fades away.

clue.text: Final defeat as pub runs dry?

explanation.surface: A drinker's despair when the pub runs out of beer.
explanation.walkthrough: Bitter is a British draught beer; when it is used up, that's the end of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Fighting to the very last, until final defeat or death; and the end of the beer supply.

clue.text: Sin, as it happens, overthrown

indicators.note: overthrown, in a down clue, turns the word upside down, so it reads from bottom to top

parts.note: a live broadcast goes out as it happens

explanation.surface: A sin being overthrown in real time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as it happens' gives LIVE; 'overthrown' turns it upside down in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Wickedness or wrongdoing in general is evil, much the same as sin.

clue.text: Rate increased — public transport needs help

parts.note: prices that have gone up have increased
BR is British Rail, the old national railway
aid is help

explanation.surface: A complaint that fares have gone up and the railways need subsidy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rate' looks like a noun (a fare rise) but is the old verb meaning to scold. BR, British Rail, ran Britain's trains when this was set.
explanation.definitionFit: To rate someone, in its old sense, is to scold or berate them severely.

clue.text: Emphasize what the teens are

explanation.surface: A teacher stresses a point about teenagers.
explanation.walkthrough: A score is twenty, and the teen numbers, 13 to 19, are all under that.
explanation.definitionFit: To stress something is to underline it; and the teens fall short of twenty.

clue.text: Philosopher successfully got home

explanation.surface: A thinker made it safely back to his house.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'bring home the bacon' is to succeed. Francis Bacon was the Elizabethan philosopher.
explanation.definitionFit: Francis Bacon the English thinker; and the prize in the idiom for winning success.

clue.text: Transport thus if trail is out of order?

indicators.note: the letters of the phrase if trail are rearranged out of their order

explanation.surface: If the overland trail is blocked, fly the goods in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of order' rearranges IF TRAIL, and 'thus' links: transport this way if the trail is closed.
explanation.definitionFit: Carrying supplies or people by aircraft is a form of transport.

clue.text: To object thus is almost excessively prim

indicators.note: almost means the word is not quite complete, so drop its final letter

parts.note: demure means modest, overly prim

explanation.surface: Someone too strait-laced to raise an objection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' trims DEMURE to its first five letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To raise an objection or show reluctance is to demur.

clue.text: Fleet Street's written about spouse with 2

indicators.note: the letters for street are written around the next piece, enclosing it

parts.note: ST is the standard abbreviation for street

indicators.note: the answer to 2 down means gradually decrease, so the spouse word loses its tail, its final letter

parts.note: a wife is a spouse

explanation.surface: A newspaper story about a journalist's wife, as if Fleet Street were the subject.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fleet Street' reads as the home of the British press, but 'Fleet' alone is the definition. 'with 2' sends you to 2 down: the spouse is docked of its tail, and 'written about' wraps the street abbreviation round it.
explanation.definitionFit: Fleet is an adjective meaning quick on one's feet, a synonym of fast.

clue.text: Rowdiness making dour men in charge mad

indicators.note: mad suggests the letters going wild and rearranging

explanation.surface: Grim men who are put in command behave badly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mad' shuffles the letters of DOUR MEN together with IC.
explanation.definitionFit: Unseemly, improper behaviour is a lack of decorum, which loud rowdiness shows.

clue.text: Inanimate deity? Nothing in it

indicators.note: the zero goes inside the deity, which 'it' refers back to

parts.note: Woden is the Anglo-Saxon chief god
nothing is zero, the letter O

explanation.surface: A sceptic says a god is lifeless, with nothing to it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it' refers back to the deity, so the O goes inside WODEN.
explanation.definitionFit: A stiff, lifeless performance is called wooden, as if made of timber and inanimate.

clue.text: Borders on row — started by French

definitions.note: plural noun in the clue, singular answer: a border region

indicators.note: the French abbreviation comes first, at the start of the rest

parts.note: a tier is a row, as of seats

explanation.surface: A dispute about a row of houses near the boundary, started by the French.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Borders' and 'row' suggest a quarrel at the boundary; 'started by' puts the French abbreviation at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: A boundary line between countries is a frontier, a border.

clue.text: Forces fellows to provide maintenance

explanation.surface: Soldiers made to look after equipment.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading is service men: workers who service machines.
explanation.definitionFit: Members of the armed forces; and repair staff who keep machinery running.

clue.text: Search for what is left in the fire perhaps

indicators.note: the letter for left is placed within the rearranged word
perhaps suggests a different form of the word fire, a rearrangement

explanation.surface: Raking the grate for whatever remains in the fire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges FIRE to RIFE, and 'in' places L inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: To rifle through something is to ransack or rummage, a thorough search.

clue.text: Meeting points where business is transacted

parts.note: E and N are compass points, east and north
a shop counter is where buying and selling is done

explanation.surface: Business people meet at points of sale.
explanation.walkthrough: Compass points are a crossword staple: any two of N, S, E and W.
explanation.definitionFit: A chance meeting with someone is an encounter.

clue.text: Lear's aged relative? Obviously not

explanation.surface: King Lear's elderly kin, unclear in the story.
explanation.walkthrough: Edward Lear wrote the nonsense poem 'Incidents in the Life of My Uncle Arly'; split the answer after the fifth letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Edward Lear's old Uncle Arly; and the adverb meaning in a vague, not obvious way.

clue.text: Frill's show-girls

parts.note: Rose is a girl's name
Marie is a girl's name

explanation.surface: Chorus girls in a composer's musical.
explanation.walkthrough: Rudolf Friml wrote the 1924 operetta Rose-Marie; the hyphen joins the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Rose-Marie is Rudolf Friml's famous operetta set in the Canadian Rockies.

clue.text: Delay when one is dismissed, perhaps

explanation.surface: An umpire holds up play when a batsman is out.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a stand is a partnership between two batsmen; when one is dismissed (out), the stand is over.
explanation.definitionFit: To let a matter remain unresolved is to postpone it; and a cricket partnership has ended when a batsman is out.

clue.text: Silk that's fashionable, in a word

explanation.surface: A stylish silk.
explanation.walkthrough: As one word it is a light glossy silk; as three it is French for in fashion, so 'in a word' tells you to run them together.
explanation.definitionFit: A thin glossy silk fabric; and the French phrase for in style.

clue.text: Men providing protection for members

explanation.surface: Men who look after the members of a club.
explanation.walkthrough: Members are limbs: chaps are the leather leggings cowboys wear over trousers to protect their legs.
explanation.definitionFit: Chaps is everyday slang for fellows, and also leather leg coverings worn by riders.

clue.text: Music for leaderless orchestra — group not up to it

indicators.note: leaderless means the orchestra loses its first letter

parts.note: the Hallé is a Manchester orchestra

indicators.note: not tells us to take away the following word up from group

parts.note: taken as written before the deletion
taken as written

explanation.surface: A conductorless band playing a piece too hard for them.
explanation.walkthrough: The Hallé is a famous orchestra based in Manchester. 'leaderless' cuts it to ALLE; 'not up' leaves GRO; 'to it' just links.
explanation.definitionFit: An allegro is a lively musical movement, a piece of music marked to be played briskly.

clue.text: Fanny without part in play's rehearsal

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the heroine's surname goes around the other piece

parts.note: Fanny Price is the heroine of Jane Austen's Mansfield Park
an act is a division of a play

explanation.surface: Fanny Price, who in Mansfield Park refuses a role in the household theatricals, at its rehearsal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' is the old sense, outside. In Mansfield Park, Fanny famously declines a role in the household play, so the surface is apt.
explanation.definitionFit: A rehearsal is a practice run before the real performance.

clue.text: Daily, pronouncement by Cockney player

indicators.note: a Londoner's Cockney vowel turns the long a into a long i

parts.note: a daily is a daily newspaper

explanation.surface: A newspaper interviews a Cockney musician.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockney speech, from East London, says 'ay' like 'eye', so a daily paper becomes this musician.
explanation.definitionFit: A bagpipe musician is a player of the instrument.

clue.text: A number about in the crowd

indicators.note: the word for about is placed inside the word the

parts.note: re means about, concerning

explanation.surface: A number of people hanging about in the crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crowd' nods to the saying that two's company and this number's a crowd.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a small number, the count after two.

clue.text: Blamed after editor's move for disorderly scene

indicators.note: the editor's letters are shifted to another spot in the word blamed

parts.note: ED is the abbreviation for editor

explanation.surface: An editor shifts the blame for chaos in the newsroom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'move' says to relocate the editor's letters within the clue's first word, not to add any.
explanation.definitionFit: Bedlam, named after a London madhouse, means a scene of uproar and chaos.

clue.text: Director, of course, is hard leaves producer

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils
an elm is a tree, which produces leaves

explanation.surface: A film director, naturally, is tough on departing producers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'producer' looks like film people; it is a tree producing leaves. 'of course' is a ship's course.
explanation.definitionFit: The tiller or wheel steers a ship's course, so it directs it.

clue.text: Plan for putting on weight

indicators.note: the word for in favour is put on, ahead of, the weight

parts.note: pro means for, in favour of
a gramme is a unit of weight

explanation.surface: A diet regime for someone who wants to gain weight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'putting on' looks like gaining pounds; here it places one piece before the other.
explanation.definitionFit: A schedule or scheme of intended activities is a plan.

clue.text: Expression of agreement from 6, perhaps

explanation.surface: A remark agreeing with clue 6.
explanation.walkthrough: Radio users say this word to mean 'received and understood'. 6 down is a philosopher; the thirteenth-century friar of that surname had this first name.
explanation.definitionFit: The radio word meaning message received and agreed; and the first name of the medieval English philosopher-friar.

clue.text: Read one novel in school

indicators.note: novel suggests something new, a fresh arrangement of the letters

explanation.surface: A pupil reads a novel at school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' rearranges READ ONE. Roedean is a famous girls' boarding school near Brighton.
explanation.definitionFit: Roedean is a well-known English independent girls' school, so an instance of a school.

clue.text: Centre of revolutionary activity on socialist occasion

definitions.text: Centre of revolutionary activity on socialist occasion

parts.words: Centre of revolutionary activity on socialist occasion
parts.note: dancers circle round a decorated post on the first of May, which is also the labour movement's festival

explanation.surface: A political rally where revolutionaries plot on May Day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolutionary' suggests politics but means going round and round; May Day is both a spring festival and the socialist labour day.
explanation.definitionFit: Dancers revolve round a ribboned post on May Day, the left's traditional holiday.
